projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Elmer Crawford was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Ian Witherspoon
sp.p: Ok we're at Elmer Crawford's house. [address redacted]. I'm Ian Witherspoon and I'm going to do this interview. Are you a veteran or a civilian?

sp.speaker: Elmer Crawford
sp.p: I'm a veteran, they gave me a discharge out of the navy, and the veterans took me in, I got veteran's rights and everything. Now I belong to the Veteran's of Foreign Wars.

sp.speaker: Ian Witherspoon
sp.p: Where did you live before the war?

sp.speaker: Elmer Crawford
sp.p: I was raised down in Oakdale California, down by Modesto.

sp.speaker: Ian Witherspoon
sp.p: Why did you want to go to Wake Island?

sp.speaker: Elmer Crawford
sp.p: Well I was working in construction, and I was working all up and down California and I couldn't save no money. Back in those days you were lucky if you made 50 cents an hour, for working. I heard about this big gold ridge up here on Butte Creek, so I went up there and got a job there as an oiler. And I was taking care of all the equipment, oiling it and greasing it and taking care of it. And I was working there when I heard about the job on Wake Island, so I went down to San Francisco and went in and told them I wanted to sign up as an oilier, they said well were not sending any oilers right now, we'll send you as a laborer. I said no, I don't want no laborer I want to go as an oiler, well they said we're not sending any right now. So I went back across the bay and I went to the North West drag line people and the guy says can I help you? I said well I hope so. I need a recommendation as an oilier. They said, what rig are you working on? I said, up in Butte Creek Canyon, on that gold ridge. We got one of your drag lines up there, were using it. Oh yeah he said, I was just up there last week, checked it all out, he said everything's good. He sit right down, wrote it all out. I took it back over to the, I gave it to the same girl on the desk and she signed me right up. 3 days later I was going out under the Golden Gate Bridge.

sp.speaker: Ian Witherspoon
sp.p: Do you remember your first days on the island?

sp.speaker: Elmer Crawford
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Ian Witherspoon
sp.p: What did it feel like to be part of the war?

sp.speaker: Elmer Crawford
sp.p: I was mostly on the fuel truck; I took care of most of the equipment on the island. I was working 10 hours a day, and I worked night shifts all the time. My base pay on the island was 145 dollars a month. But the company took care of everything. I even had a young kid make my bed. Another kid from Guam do my laundry, and I had it real good. I worked for 40 hours a week, and I was working 7 days a week, 10 hours a day. And I would work up to making 90 dollars a month bonus. Well my bonus and my overtime went to the bank in Honolulu and before I got off the boat in Seattle the company I was working for came on ship and they paid me everything I had in Honolulu. I had money hanging out of all my pockets. And I didn't have 2 pieces of my brain going in the same direction. And I was a mess.

sp.speaker: Ian Witherspoon
sp.p: Did you ever see any combat?

sp.speaker: Elmer Crawford
sp.p: Oh yeah, yep.

sp.speaker: Ian Witherspoon
sp.p: Could you tell me about some of your most memorable experiences?

sp.speaker: Elmer Crawford
sp.p: Well I was mostly carrying ammunition to the marines, but when I carried ammunition into the marine pit, if there was a marine dead there, I would pick up his riffle and use it until another marine got there to take my place.

sp.speaker: Ian Witherspoon
sp.p: You were a P.O.W.?

sp.speaker: Elmer Crawford
sp.p: Yes I was a P.O.W.

sp.speaker: Ian Witherspoon
sp.p: Did you get any medals, or awards?

sp.speaker: Elmer Crawford
sp.p: Yeah I got some medals on that discharge.

sp.speaker: Ian Witherspoon
sp.p: How did you stay in touch with your family?

sp.speaker: Elmer Crawford
sp.p: Well I couldn't right for quite a while. Then they decided that we could write to our families, and I told them were I was and everything.

sp.speaker: Ian Witherspoon
sp.p: Did you have any good luck charms?

sp.speaker: Elmer Crawford
sp.p: No

sp.speaker: Ian Witherspoon
sp.p: Do you have any pictures?

sp.speaker: Elmer Crawford
sp.p: No just those ones that that kid drew.

sp.speaker: Ian Witherspoon
sp.p: Did you keep a personal diary?

sp.speaker: Elmer Crawford
sp.p: No

sp.speaker: Ian Witherspoon
sp.p: Do you recall the day your service ended?

sp.speaker: Elmer Crawford
sp.p: Yeah I remember that real good, there was a commander in the navy, his name was Commander Stasion. Him and about 10 or 12 boats pulled up to the, I was on this prison camp on the island, out on Tokyo bay and about 10 or 12 of those little boats pulled up there and Commander Stasion walked up there and he told us guys. He said what ever you want to take with you get it, were getting out of here. And the commander of the camp, the Japanese commander, he stepped up there and said "I don't have the authority from my higher ups to release these men." And old Stasion walked right up in front of him and said "you don't need an authorization from your higher ups, I'm the highest guy around here." And I started looking for a hole to get into, because the Japs still had there riffles, I figured the shooting was about to start. It was a little scary, but those Japs backed off.

sp.speaker: Ian Witherspoon
sp.p: What did you do in the days and weeks afterwards, after you were released?

sp.speaker: Elmer Crawford
sp.p: I went out in that big hospital ship went through a battery of doctors; they took me back and put me on a plan. And we flew into Okinawa, we stayed there for a couple of days, then they flew us into the Philippines and I think I stayed there for 5 days, then they put me on a boat and sent me to Seattle Washington I was 30 days on that boat and when I got on there I weighed 150 pounds and when I got off the boat I weighed 210 pounds. First day I figured out the chow line, and I was right at the head of the line I ate and hit the tail of the line and went through again. I put on 60 pounds in 30 days. Boy I ate and ate and ate.

sp.speaker: Ian Witherspoon
sp.p: Did you have any close friendships?

sp.speaker: Elmer Crawford
sp.p: Oh yeah. I had one that when they took us from China to Japan they took about 300 of us, and I had a real close friend in there and they stopped in Osaka, and they took 150 off and they took the 1501 was in they took on up to Tokyo. Well a buddy of mine was in the 150 that stayed there, and I know his brother was there with him and he got killed, he got killed in Osaka. And I thought my buddy did too, but I come home and I took up the masonry trade. And when I got my deal from the union I started contracting. And I bid a job down in Yuba City, a big brick job. I went down there to put my materials down where I was gonna use it and here was my buddy. He was a superintendent for a general contractor out of Idaho. Then he moved to Chico and he was here until he died.

sp.speaker: Ian Witherspoon
sp.p: Did your military experience influence your thinking about war or the military in general?

sp.speaker: Elmer Crawford
sp.p: No my thoughts are all good. Right now a days I kind get upset when the democrats put so much pressure on Bush and his men. And when I was in that prison camp I saw some of my buddies get there heads cut off. I saw some of them beat to death with clubs. I got hit in the head twice with a club and bleed at the ears. And there wasn't nothing said about that. We had a democratic president at the time and there was nothing done about it. When the war was over, they didn't ask me anything about weather the Japs should pay me for working in that steel mill for 2 years. And that women back in New York her name was Linda Holms. She was a reporter. And her and a couple lawyers, that steel mill I was working in had a big contract in New York, doing the street cars and stuff. And they were putting pressure on them to pay us guys for working in that steel mill. And old Clinton went over there and told them to knock it off. He said everything was taken care of, and they all missed us. Well nobody asked me if I thought they should pay me.

sp.speaker: Ian Witherspoon
sp.p: Do you attend any reunions?

sp.speaker: Elmer Crawford
sp.p: Oh yeah. We got uh organization up in Boise Idaho called Survivors of Wake, Guam and Cavetti. Well my wife and I used to go up there all the time, but anymore we don't travel up there, we're getting too old. So I'd like to go, but I can't. I can't make it. I got Berry berry in my legs. Do you know what berry berry is?

sp.speaker: Ian Witherspoon
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Elmer Crawford
sp.p: It's caused by malnutrition. My face was all swelled up, mostly water. My legs were about that big around, mostly water. I would fall over a match stick. But I'll make it one way or another, I'll make it.

sp.speaker: Ian Witherspoon
sp.p: How did your experiences from the war affect your life?

sp.speaker: Elmer Crawford
sp.p: It didn't affect me much. I just kind of put it in the past and go on about my business. I finally took out a contractor's license; I was a contractor for about 20 years.

sp.speaker: Ian Witherspoon
sp.p: Is there anything that you would like to add that we have not gone over in this interview?

sp.speaker: Elmer Crawford
sp.p: No I don't think so. I pretty much put it all behind me. Thank you for doing this interview with me and sharing your experiences with me.
